title: Guinness Hangover: Is the Low-ABV Stout Myth True?
excerpt: Why Guinness has a reputation for rough mornings even though it's a 4.2% beer: Irish pint math, the dark-beer congener myth, bloating, and how to drink it smarter.
metaDescription: Does Guinness give you a worse hangover? Why a 4.2% stout still hits hard, how many drinks an Irish pint is, the dark-beer myth, and how to avoid it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Guinness doesn't have a special hangover-causing ingredient. A pint of Guinness Draught is actually a fairly low-strength beer, about 4.2% ABV, which is lower than many lagers and much lower than most craft IPAs. The reason Guinness has a reputation for brutal mornings is mostly about how people drink it: big Irish pints, long pub sessions, St. Patrick's Day, and the fact that a creamy, smooth stout goes down easily. If you wake up rough after Guinness, the main cause is almost always the total amount of alcohol, plus dehydration and poor sleep, not the stout itself.

**The quick rules:** Know which Guinness you're drinking (Draught is about 4.2%, Extra Stout and Foreign Extra Stout are stronger). Count Irish pints as roughly 1.35 drinks each, not one. Drink a glass of water between pints, eat a real meal before you start, and set a number before you walk into the pub. That's what makes the difference the next morning.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research about alcohol and hangovers. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. If you have a health condition, take regular medication, or are pregnant, talk to your doctor about whether drinking is safe for you.

## Is Guinness Actually Low in Alcohol? The Myth, Explained

Many people assume Guinness is strong because it looks strong. It's nearly black, it has a thick head, and it feels heavy in the mouth. That look leads to two opposite myths: that it's a "heavy" beer that will wreck you, or that it's practically a meal and so you'll be fine. Neither is quite right.

Here's how the main versions compare. Figures are typical and can vary slightly by country and year, so check the label or tap where you are.

| Guinness version | Typical ABV | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Guinness Draught (tap or widget can) | about 4.2% | The classic nitro-poured stout most people mean by "Guinness" |
| Guinness Extra Stout (bottle) | about 5.6% in the US | A sharper, more carbonated bottled stout |
| Guinness Foreign Extra Stout | about 7.5% | A stronger export stout, common in parts of Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean |
| Guinness 0.0 | essentially 0% | Alcohol-free stout made by removing the alcohol |

For comparison, a mainstream lager such as Budweiser is about 5%, and many IPAs sit between 6% and 7%. So pint for pint, Guinness Draught usually has *less* alcohol than the lager next to it at the bar. Our guide to [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) lays out more side-by-side comparisons if you want to check what else you're drinking.

The part of the myth that's true is that Guinness is easy to drink a lot of. The nitrogen pour makes it smooth with little bite, it's less fizzy than most beers, and the low strength makes people feel like they can keep going. That's exactly the setup for a hangover: not a strong drink, but a lot of a moderate one.

## Why a Guinness Hangover Can Still Hit Hard

If Guinness is relatively low in alcohol, why do so many people say it gave them their worst hangover? Several things tend to stack up.

### 1. The pint is bigger than you think

In Ireland and the UK, a pint is an imperial pint: 568 ml, or about 20 US fluid ounces. That's a quarter bigger than a 16-ounce American pint and much bigger than a 12-ounce can.

A rough way to do the math: 568 ml at 4.2% contains about 24 ml of pure alcohol, which weighs about 19 grams. A US "standard drink" is 14 grams. So one Irish pint of Guinness is about **1.35 US standard drinks**, or about **2.4 UK units**. Four pints in a Dublin pub is closer to five and a half standard drinks than four. Most people don't count that way.

### 2. The sessions are long

Guinness is the classic pub pint. People drink it at matches, at weddings, through long afternoons, and of course on St. Patrick's Day, where the drinking often starts before lunch. The total amount of alcohol over the day is what drives a hangover, and long sessions add up quietly. If your Guinness hangover follows March 17, our [St. Patrick's Day hangover guide](/never-hungover/st-patricks-day-hangover) covers the day-drinking side in more detail.

### 3. It's easy to skip water

Because Guinness is filling and not very fizzy, it's easy to think of it as "liquid bread" that takes care of itself. It doesn't. Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water), so you lose more fluid than you take in, whatever beer you're drinking. Beer does contain water, but the alcohol still pushes your body toward net fluid loss over a long night.

### 4. Mixing in other drinks

A Guinness night often doesn't stay a Guinness night. Shots of whiskey, Irish car bombs (a stout with a dropped shot of Irish cream and whiskey), or a nightcap at the end all raise the total alcohol a lot. Spirits added late in the night are a common hidden cause of a bad next morning.

### 5. Poor sleep

Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night, cutting into the deeper and dreaming stages. A late night out plus fragmented sleep is a big part of why you feel foggy and wiped out the next day, separate from anything in the glass.

## Is a Stout Hangover Different From a Lager Hangover?

People often say dark drinks give worse hangovers, and there's some real research behind the general idea. But it mostly comes from spirits, and it doesn't transfer neatly to beer.

### What congeners are and where the research comes from

**Congeners** are the chemicals in an alcoholic drink other than ethanol. They're created during fermentation and aging and include things like methanol, fusel alcohols, and various flavor compounds. In spirits, darker drinks tend to have more of them.

The best-known study, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010 by Rohsenow and colleagues, had volunteers drink bourbon or vodka to the same blood alcohol level. Hangovers after bourbon were rated somewhat worse than after vodka, though the difference was modest compared with the effect of the alcohol itself. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) walks through which drinks have the most and what the evidence really shows.

### Why that doesn't make Guinness a "high-congener" drink

The dark color in Guinness comes mainly from **roasted barley**, which is a malt-roasting effect, not the same process that loads aged spirits with congeners. Beer as a category generally sits at the low end of the congener scale compared with dark spirits. There's no good evidence that a stout, because of its color, gives a noticeably worse hangover than a pale beer at the same strength and the same amount.

If you compared four pints of Guinness Draught with four pints of a 6.5% IPA, the IPA drinker would be taking in noticeably more alcohol, and that difference would matter far more than color.

### Things that could genuinely differ

A few smaller factors can make a stout night *feel* different, even if they don't cause the hangover:

- **Fullness.** Several big pints of a creamy beer can leave your stomach feeling stretched and heavy, which can add to morning nausea.
- **Gas.** Nitrogen bubbles are small and the pour is less fizzy than most lagers, but you're still swallowing gas with every big pint.
- **Personal sensitivity.** Some people react to specific ingredients in beer, such as histamine or other compounds from fermentation, with headaches or flushing. This varies a lot from person to person and isn't unique to stout.

For a broader look at why beer hangovers in general feel heavy and bloated rather than sharp, see our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover).

## Does Guinness Make You Bloated or Gassy the Next Day?

Bloating is one of the most common complaints after a Guinness session, so it gets its own section.

**Calories aren't the main reason.** Guinness Draught is surprisingly light for how it looks. A 12-ounce serving is roughly 125 calories, which is less than many regular lagers. An Irish pint is closer to 210 calories, so the total does add up over a long session, but it isn't a calorie bomb by beer standards.

**Volume and gas are the bigger factors.** Five Irish pints is about 2.8 liters of liquid, all with dissolved gas. That stretches the stomach and can leave you puffy and uncomfortable into the next morning.

**Alcohol itself irritates the gut.** Alcohol can irritate the stomach lining and change how fast your gut moves things along, which is why loose stools and an upset stomach are common the day after any heavy drinking.

**Salty pub food piles on.** Crisps, chips, and late-night takeaway hold on to water and add to the puffy, swollen feeling.

What helps: slow down, alternate with water, eat a proper meal rather than grazing on salty snacks, and give yourself a day of normal food and fluids afterward. If your stomach is the main problem, our guide to [gas after drinking](/never-hungover/gas-after-drinking) has more practical tips.

## The "Guinness Is Good for You" Myth

"Guinness is good for you" was a famous advertising slogan from the early 20th century. For decades there were also stories of Guinness being offered to blood donors and new mothers in Ireland because of its supposed iron content. That's part of the folklore that makes Guinness feel like a healthier choice.

The reality is simpler:

- **The iron is small.** Guinness contains a little iron, but not enough to be a meaningful source compared with food. You would need to drink an unhealthy amount of beer to get much.
- **Antioxidants don't cancel alcohol.** Roasted barley contains antioxidant compounds, and you'll see headlines about beer and heart health. But any small benefit from those compounds doesn't protect you from the effects of the alcohol, and current health guidance doesn't recommend drinking for health reasons.
- **"Hearty" doesn't mean protective.** Feeling full and nourished after a stout doesn't slow down how your body processes the alcohol in any useful way. Eating a real meal before you drink does help, because food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. A pint of stout isn't a substitute for that meal.

There's also no good evidence that drinking Guinness the next morning helps a hangover. "Hair of the dog" may take the edge off for an hour because your blood alcohol rises again, but it only pushes the hangover later.

## How to Drink Guinness Without a Brutal Next Morning

The best hangover plan is the same for Guinness as for any drink: control the total amount, the pace, and what you do around it. Here's what works.

**Before you go out**

- **Eat a proper meal.** Protein, fat, and carbohydrates in your stomach slow how quickly alcohol is absorbed. Don't count the Guinness as your dinner.
- **Start hydrated.** Have a glass or two of water before you leave.
- **Pick your number.** Decide in advance how many pints you'll have, remembering that each Irish pint is about 1.35 standard drinks.

**While you're drinking**

- **One water per pint.** This is the single most useful habit. Ask for a glass of water with each round.
- **Slow down.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people. A pint of Guinness takes time to pour for a reason; take your time drinking it too.
- **Watch the extras.** Skip the late-night shots and the "one for the road" whiskey. Those often do more damage than the pints.
- **Check the strength.** If you've moved from Draught to Extra Stout or Foreign Extra Stout, you're drinking a stronger beer. Adjust.
- **Mix in Guinness 0.0.** If your pub has it, alternating with an alcohol-free stout lets you keep a pint in your hand without adding alcohol. Our page on [non-alcoholic beer and hangovers](/never-hungover/non-alcoholic-beer-hangover) explains why 0.0 drinks can't cause a true hangover.

**Before bed**

- **Drink some water.** Not a huge amount at once, just a glass or two.
- **Eat something simple if you're hungry**, but go easy on very salty or greasy food if bloating is your usual problem.
- **Skip sleeping pills or night-time cold medicines.** Combining sedating medications with alcohol can make you more impaired than you expect.

For a fuller walkthrough of the habits with the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Morning After: Recovering From a Guinness Hangover

If you're already hungover, there's no cure, but you can make the day easier.

1. **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water through the morning. An electrolyte drink can help if you were sweating or were sick. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains when they're worth it.
2. **Eat something gentle.** Toast, eggs, bananas, rice, or soup. Blood sugar can dip after drinking, and food helps with shakiness and fatigue.
3. **Treat the headache carefully.** If you use a painkiller, follow the label. Ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatory painkillers can irritate an already upset stomach, so take them with food. Be careful with acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking, and never stack it with other products that also contain it.
4. **Rest.** Your sleep was probably broken. A nap, if you can manage it, often helps more than anything else.
5. **Get some light movement.** A short walk and fresh air can help with the foggy, sluggish feeling once your stomach settles.
6. **Skip the hair of the dog.** Another pint only delays the hangover.

Most hangovers ease within about 24 hours. If you feel a lot worse than you'd expect for what you drank, or symptoms are getting worse instead of better, read the next section.

## When to See a Doctor

> **Get medical help right away (call 911 or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking:**
>
> - Can't be woken up, or is very confused
> - Has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or long gaps between breaths)
> - Has a seizure
> - Is vomiting and can't keep anything down, especially if they're also drowsy or confused
> - Has blue-tinged or very pale, cold, clammy skin
> - Has a very low body temperature
>
> These can be signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't leave the person to "sleep it off." Keep them on their side and stay with them until help arrives.
>
> **See a doctor soon if:**
>
> - You have vomiting that lasts more than a day, or you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds
> - You have severe stomach pain, especially pain that spreads to your back
> - You have black or bloody stools
> - Your symptoms haven't improved after about 24 hours or keep getting worse
> - You get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or strong anxiety when you go without drinking for a day or so. These can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Don't try to manage it alone. A doctor can help, and stopping suddenly after a long stretch of heavy daily drinking should be done with medical support.
> - You have yellowing of the skin or eyes, or dark urine

For most people, a Guinness hangover is just an unpleasant day. But these signs are not a normal hangover, and it's always better to get checked.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who drink socially add a supplement as part of their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best thought of as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that any supplement lets you drink more without consequences, and DHM doesn't replace the basics above: count your pints, drink water, and eat first.

If you want to try it, people commonly take it with their last drink or before bed. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take regular medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Guinness Draught is a lower-strength beer, about 4.2% ABV. It isn't stronger than most lagers, and it's weaker than most IPAs.
- There's no good evidence that Guinness causes a worse hangover than other beers at the same amount. The dark color comes from roasted barley, not the congeners linked to worse hangovers in spirits research.
- Guinness hangovers usually come from big pints (an Irish pint is about 1.35 US standard drinks), long sessions, added shots, skipped water, and poor sleep.
- Bloating is mostly about the volume of liquid, gas, and salty food, not calories.
- "Guinness is good for you" was a slogan, not a health finding.
- Set a number, drink water between pints, eat first, and know when a hangover is actually a sign you need medical help.

For the bigger picture, our [ranking of drinks by hangover risk](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) puts every major drink type side by side, and our guide to [congeners](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains the by-products behind the differences. Our [beer vs liquor hangover](/never-hungover/beer-vs-liquor-hangover) comparison covers how stout stacks up against spirits.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Guinness give you a worse hangover than other beers?**

Not in any way that's been shown. Guinness Draught is a fairly low-strength beer at about 4.2% ABV, which is lower than many lagers and far lower than most IPAs. There is no good evidence that Guinness specifically causes worse hangovers. When people wake up rough after a night on Guinness, the usual reasons are the number of pints, the size of those pints, and the long sessions that go with it, not something unique in the stout.

**How strong is Guinness compared with other beers?**

Guinness Draught, the one poured from a tap or a can with a widget, is about 4.2% ABV. That's close to a light-to-standard lager and well below a typical IPA (often 6 to 7%). Bottled Guinness Extra Stout is usually stronger, around 5.6% in the US, and Guinness Foreign Extra Stout is about 7.5%, so check which one you're drinking.

**How many standard drinks is a pint of Guinness?**

An Irish or UK pint (568 ml) of Guinness Draught at 4.2% contains about 19 grams of alcohol. That's roughly 1.35 US standard drinks, or about 2.4 UK units. A US 16-ounce pint is a little less, about 1.15 US standard drinks. So four Irish pints is more like five or six standard drinks.

**Why does Guinness make me feel so full and bloated?**

Guinness is poured with a nitrogen and carbon dioxide mix, which gives it the creamy head. It isn't especially high in calories (a 12-ounce serving is roughly 125 calories, less than many lagers), but the volume of liquid in several big pints, the gas, and the barley-based carbohydrates can leave you feeling heavy. Pacing and drinking water between pints helps more than switching beers.

**Is Guinness good for you, or good for a hangover?**

No. 'Guinness is good for you' was an old advertising slogan, not a health finding. Guinness does contain small amounts of antioxidant compounds from roasted barley and a little iron, but not enough to matter for health, and none of it protects you from alcohol. There is also no good evidence that drinking Guinness the morning after helps a hangover. 'Hair of the dog' only delays the hangover.

**Does Guinness have more congeners because it's dark?**

Dark color in Guinness mostly comes from roasted barley, not from the kind of congeners linked to worse hangovers in spirits research. Beer in general sits at the low end for congeners compared with dark spirits like bourbon or brandy. There's no good evidence that a stout's darker color translates into a noticeably worse hangover than a pale beer at the same strength and amount.

**Can Guinness 0.0 give you a hangover?**

No, not a true one. Guinness 0.0 has the alcohol removed and contains essentially none, so it can't cause an alcohol hangover. If you feel off after it, the likely reasons are poor sleep, a late night, dehydration from other drinks, or simply the volume of liquid and food you had.
